introduction: One image runs through the whole guide: the Manifestation of God as a gardener, humanity as his field or orchard, and each soul as a plant that is planted, watered, pruned and expected to bear fruit. The ninety-nine quotations are read here with ninety-nine from elsewhere, and the image proves to be among the oldest in scripture. God plants a garden in Eden and sets a man to dress it; Isaiah sings of a vineyard that yielded wild grapes; the psalms plant the righteous by rivers of water; Jesus speaks of sowers, tares, vines, a barren fig tree and a dresser who asks for one more year; the Qur’an coins the similitude of a goodly tree and asks who it is that fosters what is sown. Beside these stand voices that put the gardener elsewhere or doubt him. Iago makes the will its own gardener and the Dhammapada has the wise fashion themselves; Darwin admires a bank that no one tends; Blake finds a garden spoiled by its keepers; Mencius laughs at the man who pulled at his corn; Mill fears that cultivation becomes moulding. They are placed where the guide speaks of training, weeding and cutting, which are the points at which a reader may want to ask what kind of care is meant.
questions: The guide calls the Prophets gardeners of human souls. What does that image explain about education that the image of a potter, a shepherd or a physician does not?
Iago and the Dhammapada make each person their own gardener. What can a person do for their own growth, and what must come from outside?
In the parables the tares are left until harvest and the fig tree is given another year. What do these say about patience with what seems fruitless, in oneself or in others?
Blake's garden is spoiled by those who keep it, and Mill fears moulding. How would you tell cultivation from control in the raising of a child?
Darwin's entangled bank grows without a gardener. What is added, and what may be lost, when wild growth is brought into a garden?
Mencius's farmer pulls at his corn to help it grow. Where have you seen impatience do that kind of harm?

outside.why: The Song of Solomon also pictures the beloved as a garden inclosed, with a spring shut up and pleasant fruits.
Bacon begins his essay on gardens with the oldest gardener: God Almighty first planted a garden.
Genesis tells how the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden and put there the man whom he had formed.
The psalm remembers a whole people as a vine brought out of Egypt, planted, given room and caused to take deep root.
Mary at the tomb, weeping, takes the one who speaks to her for the gardener.
Pope says that education forms the mind: just as the twig is bent, the tree's inclined. Is bending a twig the same thing as cultivating it?
Plato holds that the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially with a young and tender thing.
Isaiah's song tells of a vineyard fenced, cleared of stones and planted with the choicest vine by one who looked for grapes.
The Song of Solomon greets the same turn of the year: the winter is past, the rain is over and gone, the flowers appear on the earth.
James points to the husbandman, who waits for the precious fruit of the earth and has long patience for it.
In Jesus's parable the seed springs and grows while the sower sleeps and rises, first the blade, then the ear.
Mencius tells of a man of Song who pulled at his growing corn to help it, and whose son found it all withered. What would the same impatience look like in the cultivation of a soul?
Paul calls his fellow workers labourers together with God, and the people God's husbandry.
Isaiah foresees the wilderness glad and the desert rejoicing and blossoming as the rose.
Ezekiel promises that the desolate land shall be tilled, and that people will say it has become like the garden of Eden.

Darwin contemplates an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds, insects and worms, and no gardener in view. What does the wild bank have that the garden lacks, and the garden that the bank lacks?
Shakespeare's gardener thinks it a pity that the king had not so trimmed and dressed his land as they their garden.
Iago holds that it is in ourselves that we are thus or thus: our bodies are our gardens and our wills the gardeners. Can a will tend its own garden without a gardener beyond it?
The Dhammapada says that as well-makers lead the water and carpenters bend a log, wise people fashion themselves. Where does self-cultivation end and the need of a teacher begin?
In John's Gospel the fruitless branch is taken away, and the fruitful one is purged that it may bring forth more fruit.
Isaiah compares the word to rain and snow, which water the earth and make it bring forth and bud.
In Jesus's parable a sower goes forth to sow, and the seed that falls into good ground brings forth fruit.
Isaiah says that as the garden causes the things sown in it to spring forth, so righteousness and praise will spring forth.
Isaiah's image of a soul in order is a watered garden, and a spring whose waters fail not.
Hamlet's image of a neglected world is an unweeded garden that grows to seed, possessed by things rank and gross.
Proverbs walks by the field of the slothful and finds it all grown over with thorns, and nettles covering its face.
Malachi promises those who fear the name that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing.
Paul speaks of a wild olive grafted in among the branches and partaking of the root and fatness of the tree.
In the parable the seed among the thorns is the one in whom the care of this world chokes the word, so that it becomes unfruitful.
The servants offer to gather up the tares and are told to let both grow together until the harvest, lest the wheat be rooted up with them. When is weeding the gardener's duty, and when a danger?
The first psalm likens the one who delights in the law of the Lord to a tree planted by the rivers of water.
The psalm has the righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar, planted in the house of the Lord.
Hosea hears God say: I will be as the dew unto Israel, and he shall grow as the lily.
Jeremiah's tree is planted by the waters and spreads out her roots by the river.
Isaiah gives the mourners beauty for ashes and the oil of joy, that they might be called trees of righteousness.
The Qur'an coins a similitude of a goodly tree, its root set firm and its branches reaching into heaven, giving fruit at every season.
Jesus points to the lilies of the field, which toil not, neither do they spin, and are arrayed beyond Solomon. If growth is given, what is left for the gardener and the plant to do?
Tennyson plucks a flower out of the crannies and holds it, root and all, wishing to understand it. What is the difference between studying a growing thing and tending it?
In Jesus's parable the owner of a vineyard has come three years seeking fruit on a fig tree and found none.
Paul divides the labour among the workers and gives the growth to another: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
The Qur'an asks those who cultivate whether it is they who foster what they sow, or God.
The psalm addresses God as one who visits the earth and waters it and greatly enriches it.
In the Song of Solomon the beloved says: I am come into my garden.
Isaiah foresees the fir tree coming up instead of the thorn and the myrtle instead of the brier.
The Preacher gives every thing its season, with a time to plant and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
Shelley asks the west wind: if winter comes, can spring be far behind?
Jesus says that a corn of wheat abides alone unless it falls into the ground and dies, and then brings forth much fruit.
Jesus observes that no one who has drunk old wine straightway desires new, for he says the old is better. What makes people cling to the old tree, and is all of that attachment mistaken?
Job says there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again. Is a decayed religion past such hope, or does the new planting spring from its root?
Isaiah names the vineyard as the house of Israel, a pleasant plant from which judgment was looked for and oppression found.
Jeremiah is set over the nations to root out and to pull down, to build and to plant.
The dresser of the vineyard asks that the barren tree be let alone this year also, till he dig about it and dung it. How long should a gardener wait before cutting?
Jesus gives the test for any gardener or tree: ye shall know them by their fruits.
Jesus distinguishes the good shepherd from the hireling, whose own the sheep are not, and who leaves them when the wolf comes.
Blake turns to the Garden of Love that bore so many sweet flowers and sees it filled with graves. When does the tending of a garden become the ruin of what grew there?
Jesus says that every plant which his heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up.
Jeremiah watches a potter whose vessel is marred in his hand, and who makes it again another vessel.
Hebrews admits that no chastening seems joyous at the time, but says that afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness.
Mill called a general State education a mere contrivance for moulding people to be exactly like one another. Does a gardener of children mould them, or bring out what each one is?
Moses asks that the words be taught diligently to the children, at home and by the way.
Mark tells how Jesus took the children up in his arms, put his hands upon them and blessed them.
Isaiah's shepherd gathers the lambs with his arm, carries them in his bosom, and gently leads those that are with young.
Proverbs gives the gardener's rule for children: train up a child in the way he should go.
In the parable the father sees his son a great way off, has compassion, runs, falls on his neck and kisses him.
The psalm calls children an heritage of the Lord, and the fruit of the womb his reward.
Proverbs joins the generations: children's children are the crown of old men, and the glory of children are their fathers.
Hopkins ends his complaint of barrenness with the same prayer: mine, O thou lord of life, send my roots rain.
Isaiah prays in the same posture: thou art our father, we are the clay, and we all are the work of thy hand.
Jesus says to let the little children come and forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.
Moses wishes his doctrine to drop as the rain and his speech to distil as the dew upon the tender herb.
The psalm speaks of one who shall come down like rain upon the mown grass, as showers that water the earth.
Jesus tells his disciples that he has chosen them and ordained them to go and bring forth fruit, and that their fruit should remain.
The Qur'an follows the making of a human being from a drop through clot and bones and flesh to another creation.
The psalmist asks for the same gift of speech: O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall show forth thy praise.
Jesus uses the image of himself: I am the vine, ye are the branches, and whoever abides in me brings forth much fruit.
The Qur'an likens a good gift to a grain which grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in every ear.

Candide concludes that we must take care of our garden, and Pangloss recalls that man was put into Eden to dress it. Is tending one's own plot a retreat from the world, or the beginning of its cultivation?
Paul states the farmer's law for every calling: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
The Qur'an says that the good land brings forth its vegetation by permission of its Lord.
Jesus likens the kingdom to a grain of mustard seed, the least of all seeds, which becomes the greatest among herbs.
Genesis says the Lord God took the man and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Jesus sends out seventy and says that the harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few.
Paul writes to friends that he thanks his God upon every remembrance of them, in every prayer of his.

In the parable those who have borne the burden and heat of the day complain that the last hired are made equal to them. What does working in a vineyard for love of its owner do to the reckoning of wages?
The psalm promises that they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
The Preacher says to sow in the morning and not to withhold the hand in the evening.
Paul encourages the tired worker: let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap.
Paul states the rule of the field: he which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly.
In the parable the good ground is those who keep the word in an honest and good heart and bring forth fruit with patience.
Jesus says that the harvest truly is plenteous but the labourers are few, and asks for prayer that labourers be sent.
After they have dined Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him, and tells him to feed his lambs and his sheep.
The psalm's shepherd makes his sheep lie down in green pastures and leads them beside the still waters.
Emerson says that all are needed by each one, and that nothing is fair or good alone.
Paul names the fruit a sapling of the Spirit should bear: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness.
John the Baptist warns that the axe is laid to the root, and that every tree which brings not forth good fruit is hewn down.
Marcus Aurelius has his own image of standing firm: a promontory against which the waves continually break.
Paul uses the image of fragrance for those who make the knowledge of God manifest in every place.
Marcus Aurelius admires the one who is like a vine that has produced grapes and seeks for nothing more. Does the flower need to know that the gardener is pleased?
The Qur'an points to vineyards, ploughed lands and date-palms, like and unlike, which are watered with one water.

luke-fig-tree-three-years.text: He spake also this parable; A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and he came and sought fruit thereon, and found none. Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground

matthew-every-plant-not-planted.text: But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up

isaiah-as-the-garden-causeth.text: For as the earth bringeth forth her bud, and as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth; so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all the nations

isaiah-instead-of-the-thorn.text: Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the Lord for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off

hosea-as-the-dew-unto-israel.text: I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon. His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon. They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon

genesis-planted-a-garden-eastward.text: And the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground made the Lord God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food

genesis-put-him-into-the-garden.text: And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it

song-a-garden-inclosed.text: A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed. Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits

ezekiel-like-the-garden-of-eden.text: And the desolate land shall be tilled, whereas it lay desolate in the sight of all that passed by. And they shall say, This land that was desolate is become like the garden of Eden; and the waste and desolate and ruined cities are become fenced, and are inhabited

john-supposing-him-to-be-the-gardener.text: Jesus saith unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou? She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away. Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master

corinthians-ye-are-gods-husbandry.text: For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building

luke-good-ground.text: But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience

isaiah-feed-his-flock.text: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young

isaiah-song-of-my-beloved-vineyard.text: Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes

matthew-seed-among-thorns.text: He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful

quran-watered-with-one-water.text: And in the Earth are neighbouring tracts, vineyards and ploughed lands, and date-palms, like and unlike, which are watered with one water. And we have made some of them to excel others in fruit. Lo! herein verily are portents for people who have sense.

quran-is-it-ye-who-foster-it.text: Have ye seen that which ye cultivate? Is it ye who foster it, or are We the Fosterer

bacon-god-almighty-first-planted-a-garde.text: God Almighty first planted a Garden. And indeed it is the purest of human pleasures. It is the greatest refreshment to the spirits of man
bacon-god-almighty-first-planted-a-garde.author: Francis Bacon

pope-as-the-twig-is-bent.text: 'Tis Education forms the vulgar mind; / Just as the Twig is bent, the Tree's inclin'd
pope-as-the-twig-is-bent.author: Alexander Pope

shakespeare-trimmd-and-dressd-his-land.text: O, what pity is it / That he had not so trimm'd and dress'd his land / As we this garden
shakespeare-trimmd-and-dressd-his-land.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-unweeded-garden.text: 'tis an unweeded garden, / That grows to seed; things rank and gross in nature / Possess it merely
shakespeare-unweeded-garden.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

luke-let-it-alone-this-year-also.text: And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it: And if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down

song-i-am-come-into-my-garden.text: I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice

voltaire-take-care-of-our-garden.text: Neither need you tell me,” said Candide, “that we must take care of our garden.” “You are in the right,” said Pangloss; “for when man was put into the Garden of Eden, it was with an intent to dress it: and this proves that man was not born to be idle
voltaire-take-care-of-our-garden.author: Voltaire
